props.title: Did You Hear About the Morgans?

sections.content: **Did You Hear About the Morgans?** (2009) represents one of those rare misfires in Hugh Grant's usually reliable romantic comedy career. Following the massive success of **Music and Lyrics** (2007), this fish-out-of-water comedy attempted to pair Grant with Sarah Jessica Parker fresh off her **Sex and the City** (2008) film success. The premise - a feuding New York couple forced into witness protection in Wyoming - echoes better executed city-vs-country comedies like **Sweet Home Alabama** (2002) and **Doc Hollywood** (1991).

sections.content: The film's failure highlights a crucial lesson about romantic comedy chemistry. While both Grant and Parker had proven track records individually - Grant in **Notting Hill** (1999) and **About a Boy** (2002), Parker in **Failure to Launch** (2006) - their pairing lacked the spark that made classics like **When Harry Met Sally** (1989) and **You've Got Mail** (1998) work. Director Marc Lawrence, who had success with Grant in **Two Weeks Notice** (2002), couldn't recreate the magic.

The witness protection premise also puts **Did You Hear About the Morgans?** in conversation with better executed genre-blending romantic comedies like **Miss Congeniality** (2000) and **The Proposal** (2009). These films successfully balanced their high-concept plots with genuine character development and chemistry between leads. The Morgans, unfortunately, relies too heavily on tired fish-out-of-water clichés and stereotypical portrayals of rural life. SUBHEAD: The Decline of Traditional Romantic Comedies

sections.content: The film's disappointing performance in 2009 coincided with shifting trends in romantic comedies. While the 1990s and early 2000s saw hits like **My Best Friend's Wedding** (1997) and **How to Lose a Guy in 10 Days** (2003), audiences began demanding more sophisticated takes on the genre. Films like **500 Days of Summer** (2009) and **Crazy, Stupid, Love** (2011) would soon redefine romantic comedy conventions with more complex narratives and character development.
